'Claude (this page)' is your own previous forecasts, scored the same way (its rain call counts medium or high risk as rain); use its biases to correct yourself. 'station' is the same check against EGPH's own observed daily highs and lows (METAR; complete the next day, so it includes the last week that ERA5 hasn't reached; half-hourly integer readings, so its highs run a few tenths low)

Polar vortex strength: zonal-mean zonal wind at 60°N (m/s, daily UTC mean, positive = westerly) at 10 hPa (the standard SSW level: a reversal to easterly is a major sudden stratospheric warming) and 50 hPa (lower stratosphere), per model; ensembles give mean/p10/p90/min across members and the % of members easterly. Early-warning signs from the single runs: polar_cap_t10 = area-mean temperature over 60-90°N at 10 hPa (°C; a jump of 20 °C or more in a few days is a sudden warming under way), heat_flux_100 = eddy heat flux v'T' around 60°N at 100 hPa (K m/s; sustained high values push wave energy up and tend to weaken the vortex 1-2 weeks later), waves_10hPa = amplitude in metres of zonal wavenumber 1 and 2 in the 10 hPa geopotential height around 60°N (wave 1 growing to well over 1000 m means the vortex is being displaced off the pole; wave 2 growing to several hundred metres means it is being stretched towards a split; in winter a few hundred metres each is ordinary; waves_vs_season places today against this season's analysed days). wave2_by_level gives, per single run and day, the longitude (°E, 0-180; the second ridge is 180° further east) of the wave-2 ridges in the 60°N height at 500, 100 and 10 hPa, their amplitudes, and the tilt (10 hPa ridge minus 500 hPa ridge): a ridge that shifts west with height (negative tilt, e.g. 45°E at 500, 29°E at 100, 6°E at 10 hPa) with ridges near the Urals and Alaska is the structure of a split. For ensembles, pct_members_ever_easterly is the share of members that reverse on any day of the run (the SSW probability for that window; the per-day share understates it) and reversal_median_date the typical timing. Days before 2026-11-07 are analysis.

sections.text: The Arctic Oscillation (AO) is currently negative as pressure/geopotential height anomalies across the Arctic are currently mostly positive and the AO is predicted to remain negative to neutral the next two weeks as pressure/geopotential height anomalies are predicted to remain mixed to positive the next two weeks. The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) is currently positive with mostly negative pressure/geopotential height anomalies across Greenland, and the NAO is predicted to trend negative the next two weeks as pressure/geopotential height anomalies are predicted to become mixed to mostly positive across Greenland the next two weeks. This week ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies are predicted to stretch from Scandinavia to Greenland favoring troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Central and Southern Europe. However next week as the ridging weakens across the northern North Atlantic so will the troughing across Europe. This pattern will favor normal to below normal temperatures widespread across Central and Southern Europe including the United Kingdom (UK) except for normal to above normal temperatures across Scandinavia and Northeastern Europe this week. However next week normal to above normal temperatures will become much more widespread across much of Europe including the UK. This week predicted ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across the Laptev Seas and Western Asia will favor troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies ac [...]

The widespread warmth across the Northern Hemisphere (NH) this past summer and now the fall has continued into October (see Figure). However, a series of stretched polar vortex (PV) last month has led to some, albeit modest cooling in Siberia, East Asia and to an even lesser extent far Eastern Canada and New England (see Figure). Troughing in Western Canada has also resulted in more seasonable temperatures in Western Canada (see Figure). However, the very large PV disruption developing the next two weeks does favor an overall mild pattern across the NH continents (see Figures 3, 6 and 9). The relatively cool temperatures across Siberia of October 2026 remind me of last October, though not as impressive. Last October, cold temperatures across Siberia were a precursor for more widespread cold temperatures in winter, I expect something similar for this winter but maybe of smaller magnitude. Figure. Estimate of the observed surface temperatures (°C; shading) from 01 Oct to 31 Oct 2026 based on GFS initializations and the GFS forecast from the 1 Nov 2026 run.

Let me start off this week’s blog with something that might sound like a downer and that is I don’t know all that much more what might transpire in December than I did last week. I have always felt the first important trait of a long-range forecaster is humility and what I was trying to get across most emphatically is that I don’t feel confident in what will transpire with the atmosphere through the end of the year and I don’t believe any of the models do or other human meteorologists. Of course, I can only speak for myself and is not meant to judge any peer. We all have our strengths and weaknesses; everyone is trying their best to be as accurate as possible and that should be respected. But I think with this large polar vortex disruption or sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) it will be a marathon and not a sprint (in contrast to last November’s SSW, which in the end was a sprint). It seems what might have gotten the most attention from last week’s blog is that November 2009 is the best analog for November 2026, but less attention was paid to how I started the blog and ended the blog. I started by acknowledging that a super El Niño favors a mild winter across North America and especially eastern North America. I don’t know what the true probability is, I think that it is higher than 60 or even 70 and probably 80% but I don’t think that it is 100% or very close to 100%. And I should make the distinction that I feel that the probability of a milder winter across all of Eurasia [...]

This Week The AO is predicted to be positive this week (Figure 1) with mostly negative geopotential height anomalies currently across the Arctic and mixed geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitudes of the NH (Figure 2). With predicted negative geopotential height anomalies across Greenland (Figure 2), the NAO is predicted to be positive this week. Figure 1. The predicted daily-mean AO at a) 10 hPa and at b) 1000 hPa from the 00Z 2 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. Gray lines indicate the AO index from each individual ensemble member, with the ensemble mean AO index given by the red line with squares. Ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies stretching from Scandinavia to Greenland are predicted to support troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Central and Southern Europe this week (Figure 2). This pattern will support widespread normal to below normal temperatures across much of Europe including the UK except for normal to below normal temperatures across Scandinavia, the Balkans and Turkey this week (Figure 3). This week the general pattern across Asia is ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies centered across the Laptev Sea and the Urals forcing troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across Siberia and into East Asia this week (Figure 2). This pattern favors widespread normal to above normal temperatures across Western and Southern Asia with normal to below normal temperatures across Siberia and into Northeast Asia this week (Figure  [...]

Next Week With geopotential height anomalies becoming mostly mixed across the Arctic and with mixed geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitudes this period (Figure 5), the AO will likely remain close to neutral to slightly negative this period (Figure 1). With weak and mixed pressure/geopotential height anomalies across Greenland (Figure 5), the NAO will likely also trend towards neutral to slightly negative this period. Figure 5. Forecasted average 500 mb geopotential heights (dam; contours) and geopotential height anomalies (m; shading) across the Northern Hemisphere from 8 Nov to 12 Nov 2026. The forecasts are from the 00Z 2 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. Deepening troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitude North Atlantic will support weak ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across Europe this period (Figure 5). The pattern will support the spreading of normal to above normal temperatures across Europe including the UK with the best exception for normal to below normal temperatures Central Europe this period (Figure 6). Deepening troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across the Urals will support strengthening downstream ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies centered across east Asia including Siberia this period (Figure 5). This pattern favors widespread normal to above normal temperatures widespread across much of Asia but especially Central Asia with normal to below normal temperatures limited to Eastern Si [...]

Week Two With predicted mixed to positive geopotential height anomalies across the Arctic and mixed geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitudes this period (Figure 8), the AO will likely remain near neutral to slightly negative this period (Figure 1). With predicted weak but mostly positive pressure/geopotential height anomalies across Greenland (Figure 8), the NAO will likely also remain near neutral to slightly negative this period as well. Figure 8. Forecasted average 500 mb geopotential heights (dam; contours) and geopotential height anomalies (m; shading) across the Northern Hemisphere from 13 Nov to 17 Nov 2026. The forecasts are from the 00Z 2 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. Deepening troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies across the mid-latitude North Atlantic will continue to build ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across Europe this period (Figure 8). This pattern will favor widespread normal to below normal temperatures across much of Europe including the UK this period (Figures 9). Persistent troughing/negative geopotential height anomalies centered near the Urals will support downstream ridging/positive geopotential height anomalies across East Asia this period (Figure 8). This pattern favors widespread normal to above normal temperatures across most of Asia especially Central Asia with normal to below normal temperatures limited to Eastern Siberia this period (Figure 9). Figure 9. Forecasted surface temperature anomalies (°C; shading) fr [...]

30-day Today’s polar cap geopotential height anomalies (PCHs) plot currently shows cold/negative PCHs limited to the lower troposphere with warm/positive PCHs throughout the stratosphere and mid- to upper troposphere (Figure 11). However, this week, the warm/positive PCHs in the stratosphere are predicted strengthen and eventually slowly descend into the lower troposphere. Figure 11. Observed and predicted daily polar cap height (i.e., area-averaged geopotential heights poleward of 60°N) standardized anomalies. The forecast is from the 00Z 2 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. This week the predicted cold/negative to neutral in the lower troposphere (Figure 11) are consistent with the predicted neutral surface AO (Figure 1). However, beginning next week when the warm/positive PCHs descend through the troposphere (Figure 11) the surface AO is predicted to trend slightly negative (Figure 1). Figure 12. Observed and predicted daily vertical component of the wave activity flux (WAFz) standardized anomalies, averaged poleward of 40-80°N. The forecast is from the 00Z 2 Nov 2026 GFS ensemble. The large positive (upward) pulse of vertical Wave Activity Flux (WAFz) from the troposphere to the stratosphere or poleward heat transport in the stratosphere is currently underway (Figure 12) that is triggering the large PV disruption visible in the warm/positive PCHs in the mid to upper stratosphere (Figure 11). All models including the GFS are predicting the earliest SSW on record over the next two week [...]

Arctic Sea Ice I am and will continue to watch Arctic sea ice. Current conditions are shown in Figure 16. It has been shown that less sea ice in the North Atlantic sector of the Arctic weakens the polar vortex while less sea ice in the North Pacific sector strengthens the polar vortex. Sea ice has been growing a decent clip, but clearly more in the North Pacific sector than the North Atlantic sector and therefore Arctic sea ice anomalies continue to show a strong focus or weighting of negative anomalies towards the North Atlantic sector relative to the North Pacific sector and this is a robust signal of an overall weaker PV this winter. I believe that the lack of sea ice in the Barents-Kara Seas may have contributed to the record strong high-pressure Ural/Scandinavian blocking and the unprecedentedly early weak PV that so far resembles more of an SSW than the more common stretched PV this time of year. analysis.summary:
No Met Office warnings are in force. At 08:50 the airport had 8 °C, a light variable wind, broken cloud at 3300 ft and 1024 hPa. The night was dry, with a low of 7 °C.

A weak high keeps Saturday to Tuesday grey, mild and mostly dry. On Wednesday 11 November a low passes south of us, and only UKMO brings clear rain here.

Behind the low, a cold northerly gives clear skies and frost on 12-14 November, with icy patches on wet surfaces. Atlantic wind and rain return from 15-16 November.

High above us, the 60°N wind at 10 hPa reverses on 10-12 November in 100% of members of all four ensembles. It is the earliest major SSW on record.

stratosphere.winter_impact:
The reversal on about 10-12 November is near certain, the earliest major SSW in the record. It is short at 10 hPa. The lower stratosphere stays weak for longer, but less so than in yesterday's runs.

The event grew from below. A strong Ural-Scandinavian block over open Barents-Kara water (+1.96 °C) pushed waves into a young vortex. The block ends on 9-10 November, so the push stops.

About two thirds of major SSWs reach the troposphere, usually 1-3 weeks later. For this event that window is about 17 November to early December.

For a surface response:
- The GFS 1000 hPa cap is +0.7 sd on 17-18 November.
- ECMWF has Blocking plus NAO- near 50% on 27-29 November and Blocking at 28-35% on 2-7 December. Its weekly maps have high pressure over Greenland on 30 November to 7 December and on 14-21 December.
- The SEAS5 November issue has NAO medians of about -1.5 to -3.0 from November to February. Seasonal models understate the NAO, so I give this signal extra weight.

Against a response:
- The 50 hPa wind stays westerly, and the heat flux is near normal after 7 November.
- GEFS has only 0-3% of members at +1 sd at 100 hPa after 9 November. The GFS 1000 hPa cap turns to -1.1 to -1.2 sd on 22-23 November.
- ECMWF has NAO+ as the largest regime at 37-49% on 15-25 November.
- The 10 hPa wind rebuilds to about 38-43 m/s in December, above its model climate. The westerly QBO (+15.9 m/s at 30 hPa) helps that rebuild.

The northerly on 12-14 November comes from the troposphere, as the block ends and a ridge builds to our west. It is too early to be a downward response.

For Edinburgh:
- A response in late November or early December most likely brings frost and fog under a high, or a northerly with snow on the Pentlands.
- The North Sea is +0.99 °C against 1991-2020, so snow at the coast needs colder air aloft than usual.
- A strong vortex in mid-December favours mild, wet westerlies.

My view is wrong if most members put the 100 hPa cap back above +1 sd after 20 November and the AO stays below -1 into early December.

winter_outlook.summary:
My call: a near-normal winter with a slight tilt to mild. The best cold chances are 10-16 November, late November to mid-December, and February. Confidence is low.

The odds:
- December to February colder than its 1991-2020 normal: 29% (medium).
- At least one proper cold spell from 1 November to 31 March: 44% (medium). A spell is 5 or more days in a row, each with a minimum of -3 °C or lower or 5 cm of lying snow.
- A major sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) that starts in November: 97%. December 4%, January 15%, February 22%.

The polar vortex is at a record low for the date. The 60°N 10 hPa wind is 2.5 m/s in the analysis for 00 UTC on 7 November. The weakest value for the date in the NASA record is 12.6 m/s. All four ensembles turn the wind easterly on 10-12 November, in 100% of their members. Then the upper vortex rebuilds fast and is stronger than normal by early December.

The lower stratosphere now stays disturbed for a shorter time than in my last run. But the GEFS AO and NAO forecasts for 10-16 November are deeper, and the ECMWF week to 16 November is colder. The warm seas, the westerly QBO and the mild air upwind still lean mild. The strongly negative SEAS5 NAO and the December blocking signal still lean cold. These signals balance, so my odds change little.
winter_outlook.reasoning:
BASE RATES (source winter_base, ERA5-Land at the point, exact definitions):
- 1991-2020: 40% cold DJF, 43% cold spell.
- Last 15 winters (2011/12 to 2025/26): 27% and 40%.
- All winters since 1950/51: 57% and 61%. The colder early decades push these up.

I start from 1991-2020, because the DJF normal of 3.97 °C uses that period. I move towards the last 15 winters because of the warm trend. The CET has June to October 2026 at +1.1 to +2.7 °C, with ranks 349 to 367 of 368 from the coldest. My start is 33% for a cold DJF and 42% for a cold spell. The base-rate source has data only to 1 November, with no spell days yet.

1) STRATOSPHERIC VORTEX: 0 on DJF, +3 on the spell.

Strength:
- The 60°N 10 hPa wind is 2.5 m/s in the analysis for 00 UTC on 7 November (severe-weather.eu). That is 23.3 m/s below the mean for the date.
- Weatheriscool gives 2.6 m/s, against an ERA5 weakest value of 12.9 m/s for the date (2016).
- The NASA analysis ends on 4 November at 1.3 m/s, a record low for the date. NASA's climatology for 7 November has a minimum of 12.6 m/s, a 10th percentile of 17.0 m/s and a mean of 26.9 m/s.
- GEOS-FP, one of the two sources for the score, has the first easterly day on 10 November and a low of -3.4 m/s on 11 November. It is westerly again at 2.7 m/s on 13 November.

Reversal shares (numeric member counts, any day of the run):
- ECMWF ENS: 100%, median first reversal 10 November, 100% easterly on 10-12 November, lowest member -3.6 m/s.
- AIFS ENS (machine learning): 100%, median 11 November, 92% easterly on 11 November, lowest member -2.9 m/s.
- GEFS (NOAA, 7 November 00Z): 100%, median 11 November, 100% easterly on 11-12 November, lowest member -3.9 m/s.
- GEPS: 100%, median 11 November, 100% on 11-12 November and 81% on 13 November, lowest member -5.0 m/s.
- Severe-weather.eu gives 100% for all three of its ensembles. Weatheriscool gives only 26% for ECMWF ENS. That figure disagrees with every numeric member count, so I think it comes from another run or window. I use the numeric 100%.

Deterministic runs: ECMWF HRES reaches -2.7 m/s on 11 November, GFS -3.2 m/s, AIFS (machine learning) -2.9 m/s, GEM -2.8 m/s, UKMO -2.6 m/s and ARPEGE -1.5 m/s on 10 November. The GFS section has easterlies down to 20 hPa on 11 November. The physics models and the machine-learning models agree.

Recovery:
- Numeric means: ECMWF ENS 13.8 m/s and AIFS ENS 14.3 m/s on 21 November. GEPS 23.0 m/s and GEFS 26.9 m/s on 23 November. The NASA mean for 23 November is 29.3 m/s.
- ECMWF 46-day chart (6 November run), my reading: all members near 0 to -3 m/s on about 10-12 November. This agrees with the numeric 100%.
- The chart mean reaches about 25 m/s by 23 November and crosses the model-climate mean (about 32 m/s) near 27 November. It reaches about 37 m/s by 4 December, 40 m/s by 11 December and 43 m/s by 21 December, against a model-climate mean of 33-35 m/s.
- One member drops to about 10 m/s near 6 December. One member turns easterly near 19-20 December and reaches about -12 m/s on 21 December. That is about 1% of the members, from my chart reading, not from numeric data.

ECMWF weekly 10 hPa temperature anomalies (6 November run):
- 9-16 November: warm over the pole, about +15 to +30 °C.
- 23-30 November: cold over Canada and Greenland (-5 to -10 °C), slightly warm near Scandinavia.
- 7-14 December: a cold pole, about -5 to -15 °C. The vortex is strong.

Shape:
- Wave 2 came first: 585-596 m on 2 November in every model. Its ridges sat at 38-40°E at 500 hPa, 31-32°E at 100 hPa and 5°E at 10 hPa. That is a westward tilt of 33-35° with height, the structure of a split.
- Wave 2 then falls to 46-76 m on 10-11 November. Wave 1 grows from 598-610 m today to 769-839 m on 13-19 November. The event becomes a displacement.
- ECMWF ENS-mean 10 hPa maps (7 November run): on 12 November the main low sits off the pole towards northern Europe, with a small second low on the Pacific side. On 17 November the cold core is an oval from Greenland across Scandinavia towards the Urals. On 22 November one large low sits near the pole, shifted to the Barents-Kara side.
- Hebweather centroids: ECMWF 60.6-62.6°N on 8-10 November, then 65.6-69.6°N. GFS stays at 61-70°N. This confirms a displacement and a return.
- No GFS or AIFS 10 hPa hemispheric map was readable in this run. Their shape comes from the wave numbers, which show the same sequence in all models.
- Late in the runs, a weak split-type structure comes back. ECMWF HRES has wave-2 ridges at 69-75°E at 500 hPa and 58-60°E at 100 hPa on 20-21 November, with a tilt of -65 to -82°. AIFS has 40-49°E and 20-39°E on 18-21 November. The amplitudes are only 85-190 m.

Depth: the two measures disagree.
- The 50 hPa wind stays westerly: ECMWF ENS mean 6.6 m/s today and 5.3 m/s at its weakest on 12 November. 0% of members in ECMWF ENS, GEFS, AIFS ENS and AIGEFS turn it easterly. The lowest single member is 0.7 m/s (AIFS ENS).
- The polar cap is very high: +4.25 sd at 10 hPa, +2.78 sd at 50 hPa and +1.83 sd at 100 hPa in the ECMWF HRES analysis today. The 100 hPa peak was +2.19 sd on 4 November.
- 100% of members in all four ensembles are above +1 sd at 100 hPa today. By the cap rule, the event is deep. It reaches the lowest stratosphere.

Persistence at 100 hPa, share of members above +1 sd:
- ECMWF ENS: 39% on 10 November, 6% on 12 November, 35-39% on 15-17 November, 25-33% on 18-21 November.
- AIFS ENS: 6-41%, with 41% on 21 November.
- GEPS: 0% on 11-15 November, then 29-43% on 19-23 November.
- GEFS: 0-3% from 10 November.
- This is less than in my last run, when ECMWF ENS had 45-55% on 16-20 November.

Surface link:
- The GFS section has the 1000 hPa cap at +0.72 sd and the 500 hPa cap at +0.60 sd on 17 November. Then both fall to -1.19 sd and -1.33 sd on 22 November.
- The ECMWF HRES 500 hPa cap falls to -1.26 sd on 20 November, and GEM has -1.29 sd on 16 November.
- So the link to the surface is short. A low polar cap in the troposphere in late November is a positive-AO sign.

Early-warning signs:
- The ECMWF HRES 10 hPa polar-cap temperature rose from -59.5 °C on 2 November to -55.0 °C on 7 November. That is only 4.5 °C, a push from the waves and not a classic sudden warming. NASA put it above the 90th percentile on 4 November.
- It cools to -68.3 °C by 21 November, near the NASA mean of -67.0 °C for that date.
- The 100 hPa heat flux was 32-40 K m/s on 2-4 November and is 13.3 K m/s today. Severe-weather.eu gives 12.7 K m/s against a mean of 11.3 and a 90th percentile of 18.2, so it is near normal now. The NASA 45-day mean is 11.6 K m/s, a record high for the date.
- ECMWF HRES has a second pulse of 26.5 K m/s on 21 November. In my last run it had 32.4 K m/s on 20 November, so the pulse is smaller. GFS peaks at 17.0 K m/s and AIFS at 18.5 K m/s. One run at day 14 is only an early signal.

What ties it together:
- A record Ural-Scandinavian block over open Barents-Kara water (+1.96 °C) drove wave 2 upward in late October.
- A November vortex has little inertia, so a moderate push reversed it. The push stopped about 5 November, so the upper vortex rebuilds fast.
- The lower stratosphere stays high for a shorter time than I expected last run. The troposphere over the pole turns low again by 20-22 November.
- So the surface effect falls mostly on 9-17 November. That fits the deep GEFS AO and the colder ECMWF week to 16 November.
- The record has no case like this. It is the earliest major SSW since at least 1979. The nearest case is 1987/88 (El Niño, westerly QBO, SSW on 8 December), and Edinburgh had a DJF anomaly of +0.2 °C.

I give 0 on DJF, down from +1, because the lower stratosphere stays disturbed for less time. I give +3 on the spell, down from +4, because the short link to the surface falls in November, which counts for the spell.

2) SUPER EL NIÑO: -1 on DJF.
- Niño 3.4 is +3.4 °C (week of 28 October). The ONI is +2.46 for August to October.
- The SEAS5 plume (1 November) peaks near +4.0 to +4.1 °C in December and January against ERA5 1991-2020, then falls to about +3.1 °C in March.
- It favours a mild, stormy early winter and a negative-NAO tilt late in the winter. I count the late-winter part inside the SEAS5 NAO point, as last time, so that I do not count it twice.

3) QBO WESTERLY: -4 on DJF, -3 on the spell.
- 30 hPa +15.91 m/s and 50 hPa +13.45 m/s in October. The westerly phase fills both levels.
- It favours a strong vortex, a fast rebuild and fewer mid-winter SSWs.

4) MJO: 0 on both.
- Phase 4 from 24 October to 2 November, with the amplitude down from 1.40 on 27 October to 0.57 on 2 November. It is weak, so it gets no weight.

5) AAM AND GWO: 0 on DJF, +1 on the spell.
- Relative AAM is +0.52 sd on 6 November, down 0.92 in 7 days and the lowest in 90 days. It was +3.55 sd on 20 September.
- The GWO is in phase 7 with amplitude 0.77 on 4 November, so it is weak. Its tendency is near 0 (-0.02 sd).
- A fall after a high often comes with ridges and blocks 1-2 weeks later, so about 13-20 November. That fits the GEFS NAO- on 10-16 November. It is one fall inside a super El Niño, so I do not over-read it.

6) SEA TEMPERATURES:
- OISST against 1991-2020: subpolar -0.43 °C (25% of cells below -1 °C), subtropical +0.92 °C (54% above +1 °C), tripole -1.35. That is the positive-NAO pattern. Tropical Tidbits (against 1981-2010) shows the same cold water south of Greenland. -2 on DJF.
- North Sea +0.99 °C, with 57% of cells more than 1 °C above normal. Seas around Scotland +0.57 °C. An easterly gives heavier showers, but snow at the coast is marginal. -1 on the spell.
- Barents-Kara open water +1.96 °C, with 79% of cells above +1 °C. It links to a weak vortex. +1 on both.
- GOES boxes (against 2003 on): Gulf Stream +0.41 °C, Sargasso +0.98 °C, Mid-Atlantic Bight +2.03 °C, Gulf of Maine +1.14 °C. Background only.

7) SNOW COVER AND THE UPWIND COLD POOL: -1 on DJF, -2 on the spell.
- Weekly extent (week 44): Eurasia 14.55 against a normal of 16.06 million km² (rank 41 of 61), up 2.0 in a week. The hemisphere is 23.98 against 27.62 (rank 46).
- The departure map has 91 Eurasian cells with more snow than usual, mostly in Siberia, and 110 with less. The ground is bare from western Russia to Scandinavia.

Upwind cold pool (ECMWF ENS to 21 November), peak share of members at -8 °C at 850 hPa:
- Moscow 100% on 7 November and 84% on 11 November. Kyiv 100% on 7 November. Both sit south-east of our usual track.
- Helsinki 20% on 20 November, Stockholm 12% on 21 November, Oslo 10% on 19 November, Copenhagen 2%.
- At -5 °C the shares are higher: Oslo 53%, Stockholm 59% and Copenhagen 31% on 14 November, Helsinki 63% on 15 November.
- Snow cover reaches only 8% of members at Oslo and 0% at Stockholm, Helsinki and Copenhagen.

Oslo is less cold than in my last run (10% against 14-16%, with snow cover 8% against 18%). The source air is not cold enough for snow to low levels here. So I take one more point off the spell.

TROPOSPHERE.

AO and NAO (NOAA, GEFS from 6 November):
- AO observed: +1.25 on 28 October, -0.66 on 6 November. The forecast mean falls to -1.57 on 11 November and -1.74 on 12 November, with 100% of members negative on 9-13 November. It stays below -1 to 15 November and is near 0 from 18 November.
- NAO observed: -0.05 on 6 November. The forecast mean is -0.55 to -1.14 on 10-15 November, with 97-100% of members negative. It is -0.61 on 16 November and -0.19 to -0.37 on 17-21 November.
- That is about 7 days of NAO below -0.5. It is deeper than in my last run, but it is still not two weeks.

ECMWF regimes (6 November run):
- Blocking 100% on 6-9 November.
- Atlantic Ridge is the largest regime on 10-14 November (about 50-60%). That gives a northerly component on its eastern side.
- NAO+ is the largest regime on 15-24 November, at 41-49%, with 49% on 19 November.
- From about 27 November to 10 December, Blocking plus NAO- is about 45-51%, with Blocking itself at 22-35%. NAO+ falls to 20-33%.
- For 11-20 December, Blocking plus NAO- is about 36-46%. This is slightly less than the 49-57% of my last run.

Simon Lee's index (5 November run):
- Scandinavian blocking falls from +1.2 sd on 7 November to about -0.5 sd on 12 November.
- NAO- peaks at +1.2 sd on 12 November, falls to +0.3 sd near 22 November, then rises to about +0.6 sd by mid-December.
- NAO+ rises from -1.2 sd to about +0.1 sd on 17 November, then stays at -0.3 to -0.5 sd in December.
- The two schemes agree on the end of the block about 10-12 November. They agree on a shift away from NAO+ about 27 November. In mid-November, Lee leans NAO- while ECMWF leans Atlantic Ridge, then NAO+.

Hovmöller (6 November run, 35-60°N):
- In the analysis, a ridge sat near 0-20°E on 1-4 November.
- A strong trough sits at 10-40°E on about 6-11 November, with a ridge at 50-75°E. The ridge to our west sits far out over the Atlantic, so the northerly window here on about 9-12 November is weak and short.
- A trough moves east from 50°W and reaches 0° on about 17-19 November.
- From about 22 November to 8 December the anomalies are weak. Weak ridges lie over 0-50°E and a weak trough near 25-50°W. That set-up gives south-westerlies here.

ECMWF weekly anomalies (6 November run):
- 16-23 November: a deep low over Scotland and Ireland (-10 to -20 hPa) and a 500 hPa trough to the north-west. Scotland near normal, England 0 to +1 °C. That is a stormy NAO+ week.
- 30 November to 7 December: high pressure over Greenland (+5 to +10 hPa), slight low pressure over the UK and central Europe. Scotland near normal.
- 7-14 and 14-21 December: Scotland near normal, England 0 to +1 °C. The 14-21 December map has a Greenland high and low pressure south-west of the UK.

Edinburgh meteogram (6 November run), weekly 2 m medians: about -2 °C for the week to 16 November, colder than the -0.5 °C of my last run. Then about 0 to +0.5 °C each week to 21 December. MSLP is about +3 hPa first, then about -12 hPa in the week to 23 November. I count -1 on DJF for the near-normal to mild December weeks. I count +1 on the spell for the colder week to 16 November.

SEASONAL MODELS:
- The C3S, meteociel SEAS5 and GloSea maps are the October issue. They were run before this event and do not include it.
- C3S: the UK +0.5 to +1 °C in November to January, near normal in Scotland in February and March, and about 10% wetter. GloSea DJF: the UK about +0.5 to +1 °C.
- The ECMWF SEAS5 November issue started on 1 November. The vortex was already very weak then, but it was before the reversal.
- SEAS5 November terciles: Scotland mostly 60-100% above the upper tercile for DJF and JFM. Its DJF precipitation is wetter over much of the UK.
- SEAS5 November DJF MSLP: +2 to +4 hPa over Greenland and Iceland, -2 to -4 hPa over the UK. That is a negative-NAO pattern with a storm track to the south.
- SEAS5 November NAO medians: November -1.6, December -1.6, January -1.9, February -3.0, March -2.4. The model-climate medians are near 0. This is a strong signal, and seasonal models understate the NAO.
- SEAS5 point data (raw, about 1° grid, not bias-corrected), members milder than normal: November 37%, December 45%, January 55%, February 49%, March 37%. December is lower than the 57% in my last run. February has 10 frost days against 8.3, and March 8 against 5.7.

The SEAS5 NAO and MSLP say colder. The terciles say warmer, because the continent and the seas are warm. An easterly from a mild continent does not give a cold month. I give +5 on DJF for the NAO and MSLP signal and -2 for the warm terciles. I give +1 on DJF for the point data, because about half of the members are colder than normal in DJF. On the spell, I give +3 and -1.

ANALOGS AND CET:
- The autumn-matched analogs are 1987/88, 2006/07, 2015/16, 2004/05 and 1982/83. Their mean DJF is +0.3 °C, 1 of 5 is colder, and 2 of 5 had an SSW (40% against 57%).
- Their chance_check is within chance (detrended mean +0.45 °C, random 5-95% range -0.69 to +0.66 °C). So they do not move the odds. None had a November reversal.
- The early-SSW set has only 4 winters: 1981/82 (-2.1 °C), 1987/88 (+0.2 °C), 1998/99 (+0.3 °C) and 2001/02 (+0.5 °C). Its mean is -0.3 °C, 1 of 4 is colder, and none started in November. It is within chance.
- Three of the four had an easterly QBO (-9.5 to -18.2 m/s) and La Niña or neutral ENSO. Only 1987/88 resembles this year. I weight this set down and do not move the odds.
- Severe-weather.eu lists other analogs (2016/17, 2009/10, 1977/78, 1960/61, 1958/59), with 1 SSW winter in 5 against a 53% base rate. They do not resemble this winter.
- CET: a cold November leads to a cold DJF 38% of the time, against a 33% base rate (correlation 0.09). A cold November carries little weight.
- CET context: 2009/10 was -2.35 °C and 1962/63 -5.21 °C against 1991-2020. At Edinburgh the recent cold winters were only -0.3 to -0.7 °C (2012/13, 2014/15, 2017/18, 2020/21). A small cold anomaly is enough for a cold DJF.

MET OFFICE (11 November to 5 December):
- Rain clears from the south and clearer air spreads from the north, with a few wintry showers in the far north. Then from the weekend of 14-15 November, Atlantic fronts bring rain and strong winds. After a cold start, temperatures are above average. Late November is unsettled, perhaps drier into early December, and above normal.
- I agree on the timing. The cold start fits the GEFS NAO- and the -2 °C ECMWF week. The change at the weekend fits the NAO+ regime from 15 November and the -12 hPa MSLP week.
- I differ a little for early December. The ECMWF weeklies keep Scotland near normal under a Greenland high, so I do not expect above normal there.

AER (Judah Cohen, 2 November, 5 days old):
- I agree on the earliest SSW on record and on his low confidence about December. His forecast of normal to below normal UK temperatures for 13-17 November fits the GEFS and ECMWF data.
- He calls the event 'a marathon and not a sprint'. The 10 hPa vortex rebuilds by late November, and the 100 hPa cap stays above +1 sd in only 25-39% of ECMWF members after 15 November. So I disagree for both levels now.
- I do not use November 2009 as an analog. That winter had no November reversal, and its SSW came on 9 February 2010.
- His cold-Siberia argument gets weak support. Siberia has more snow than usual, but the Eurasian extent ranks 41 of 61.

SSW BY MONTH (reference rates November 2%, December 10%, January 22%, February 22%):
- November 97%: all four ensembles have 100% of members easterly, and GEOS-FP itself forecasts -3.4 m/s on 11 November. The ensemble-mean minima are now -2.7 to -3.1 m/s, deeper than in my last run. I keep 3% back because the reversal lasts only about 3 days. A return to 10 westerly days before 30 April is near certain.
- December 4%: a new event cannot start until 20 westerly days after the last easterly day, so about 2-3 December. The ECMWF 46-day chart has about 1 member in 100 easterly near 19-20 December. The westerly QBO and the strong rebuild keep this below the reference rate.
- January 15%: the westerly QBO and a strong rebuilt vortex, against El Niño wave forcing and the smaller late-November heat-flux pulse.
- February 22%: El Niño forcing late in the winter and the SEAS5 February NAO of -3.0 balance the westerly QBO. I keep the reference rate.
- Other people's dated SSW calls do not move these numbers.

NET:
- DJF: 33 +0 (vortex) -1 (El Niño) -4 (QBO) -2 (tripole) +1 (Barents-Kara) -1 (snow cover and cold pool) -1 (ECMWF weeklies) +5 (SEAS5 NAO and MSLP) -2 (warm terciles) +1 (SEAS5 point data) +0 (analogs, CET, AAM, MJO) = 29%.
- Spell: 42 +3 (vortex) -3 (QBO) +1 (AAM) -1 (North Sea) +1 (Barents-Kara) -2 (snow cover and cold pool) +1 (colder week to 16 November) +3 (SEAS5 NAO) -1 (warm terciles) +0 (analogs, MJO) = 44%.
- I differ from the SEAS5 and C3S temperature maps, because I weight their own negative NAO more. I differ from AER on the length of the disruption. I do not let the analogs move the odds.

WHAT CAN MAKE ME WRONG:
- Colder: the GEFS AO of -1.7 comes true and the high pressure over Scandinavia and Greenland stays longer than ECMWF shows. Then 10-16 November can give 5 frosts in a row. The December blocking can then join a negative-NAO February.
- Milder: the rebuilt vortex goes very strong, the QBO keeps the jet fast, and the December blocks sit over Scandinavia with southerlies here. Then even 44% for the spell is too high.

PREVIOUS OUTLOOK (29% and 43%), sign by sign:
1. Colder (half or more of ECMWF ENS and GEPS members above +1 sd at the 100 hPa cap on 18-28 November, with the observed AO below -1 for 5 or more days by 5 December): mixed. The cap part moves away: ECMWF ENS has 25-33% on 18-21 November and GEPS 10-43%. The AO part is on track in the forecast only: GEFS has the AO below -1 on 10-15 November.
2. Colder (runs on 10-15 November confirm a heat-flux pulse above 30 K m/s on 19-25 November, and more than 20% of 46-day members below 20 m/s in early December): those runs are not out yet. Today the HRES pulse is smaller (26.5 K m/s), and only a few 46-day members fall below 20 m/s. It moves away.
3. Colder (ECMWF runs from 9 to 30 November keep Blocking plus NAO- above 45% on most days of 1-20 December, with a Scandinavian or Greenland high on the weekly maps): those runs are not out yet. The 6 November run has 45-51% to 10 December and 36-46% after. It has a Greenland high on the weekly MSLP maps. Partly on track.
4. Colder (more than 30% of members at -8 °C over Oslo or Stockholm with snow cover above 20% by 30 November): not yet, and it moves away. Oslo has 10% with 8% snow cover, and Stockholm 12% with 0%.
5. Colder (the SEAS5 December issue keeps the January and February NAO below -1.5, and the Scotland DJF tercile turns neutral): cannot be judged until about 5 December.
6. Colder (AAM below 0 sd and the GWO in phases 1-3 by 30 November): not yet, but it moves that way. AAM is +0.52 sd and falls, and the GWO is weak in phase 7.
7. Milder (ECMWF ENS mean 10 hPa wind above 40 m/s by 10 December, a cold pole, heat flux below 12 K m/s): on track in the forecast, with about 40 m/s near 11 December and a cold pole on 7-14 December. Not yet observable.
8. Milder (NAO+ above 45% on several days in successive runs for late November into December, and the December blocking gone): half met. The 6 November run has NAO+ at 47-49% on 19-21 November. But NAO+ is only 20-33% in December, and the blocking stays.
9. Milder (the Edinburgh week to 16 November ends near or above normal, with no run of 3 or more nights at -3 °C or lower by 20 November): it moves away. The meteogram now has about -2 °C. Not observable until 16-20 November.
10. Milder (the SEAS5 December issue drops the NAO signal): cannot be judged until about 5 December.

SOURCES OF THE CHANGE:
- DJF stays at 29%. The weather gave a shorter disturbance in the lower stratosphere, so the vortex point went from +1 to 0. The SEAS5 point data now has fewer mild members in December, so I add 1 point. The two changes cancel.
- The spell went from 43% to 44%, because of the weather. The week to 16 November is colder and the GEFS AO is deeper. The weaker upwind cold pool and the shorter lower-stratosphere disturbance take most of that back.
- I did not reweigh old evidence in this run. Each change comes from new data.
cold_windows: 10-16 November (medium for frost, low for a qualifying spell): frost under high pressure, with a weak northerly component. GEFS has the AO near -1.7 on 12 November and the NAO below -0.5 on 10-16 November. The ECMWF week to 16 November is about 2 °C below normal. The Met Office expects fine, dry weather with a few wintry showers in the far north, then Atlantic fronts from about 14-15 November. In the city: frost, fog and ice on untreated paths on clear nights. Some nights can reach -3 °C, but five in a row is unlikely before the fronts arrive. On the Pentlands: hard frost and a thin cover of snow from showers.

February (medium): blocking with easterlies or battleground snow. SEAS5 November has an NAO median of -3.0, and its DJF MSLP has high pressure over Greenland and low pressure over the UK. Late-winter El Niño forcing points the same way. The North Sea is warm (+0.99 °C), so the coast needs 850 hPa near -8 °C for snow, not sleet. In the city: snow that settles for a day or two in the best case. On the Pentlands: lying snow for days.

27 November to 20 December (low-medium): blocking with a Greenland high. ECMWF has Blocking plus NAO- at 45-51% on 27 November to 10 December, and its weekly maps have a Greenland high on 30 November to 7 December and 14-21 December. Scotland is near normal on those maps, not cold. A northerly favours north-east Scotland more than the Lothians. In the city: sleet, wet snow and icy surfaces at times. On the Pentlands and Moorfoots: snow with some lying cover.

March (low-medium): SEAS5 has an NAO median of -2.4, only 37% of members milder and 8 frost days against 5.7. In the city: late frosts and short snowfalls. On the hills: lying snow after northerly or easterly outbreaks.
January (low): mostly westerly behind a strong vortex. Snow showers from polar-maritime air on the hills and frost on clear nights in the city. Snow to low levels needs a block.
would_change: Colder: the observed AO stays below -1 for 5 or more days on 10-17 November, and ECMWF ENS keeps 40% or more of its members above +1 sd at the 100 hPa polar cap on 20-30 November.
Colder: Edinburgh has 3 or more nights in a row at -3 °C or lower on 11-16 November. Then a qualifying spell in November becomes a real chance.
Colder: ECMWF extended runs from 9 to 30 November keep Blocking plus NAO- above 45% on most days of 27 November to 20 December, with a Greenland or Scandinavian high on the weekly MSLP maps.
Colder: two or more models show a 100 hPa heat-flux pulse above 25 K m/s on 19-28 November, and more than 10% of ECMWF 46-day members stay below 20 m/s in December.
Colder: by 30 November, 30% or more of ECMWF members at -8 °C at 850 hPa over Oslo or Stockholm, with snow cover in 20% or more of members.
Colder: the SEAS5 December issue (about 5 December) keeps the January and February NAO medians below -1.5, and the Scotland DJF tercile turns neutral.
Colder: AAM below 0 sd and the GWO in phases 1-3 by 30 November.
Milder: the ECMWF ENS mean 10 hPa wind above 40 m/s by 10 December, with a cold pole and the 100 hPa heat flux below 12 K m/s.
Milder: NAO+ above 45% on most days of 20 November to 10 December in successive ECMWF extended runs, and the December blocking signal gone.
Milder: the Edinburgh week to 16 November ends near or above normal, with no night at -3 °C or lower.
Milder: the SEAS5 December issue drops the NAO signal, with January and February medians above -0.5.
snow_checklist: ✅ Polar vortex weakens or breaks down: the 60°N 10 hPa wind is 2.5 m/s in the analysis on 7 November, against a NASA minimum of 12.6 m/s for the date. 100% of members in ECMWF ENS, AIFS ENS, GEFS and GEPS turn it easterly on 10-12 November. ECMWF rebuilds it to about 37-43 m/s by 4-21 December.

🟡 AO/NAO negative for 2+ weeks: the AO is -0.66 and the NAO -0.05 on 6 November. GEFS has the AO at -1.57 to -1.74 on 11-12 November and the NAO below -0.5 on 10-16 November, then both near 0. That is about 7-9 days, not 2 weeks. SEAS5 November gives NAO medians of -1.6 to -3.0 for December to February.

🟡 Blocking high over Scandinavia or Greenland: a Scandinavian block is in the analysis now (ECMWF Blocking 100% on 6-9 November, Lee's index +1.2 sd on 7 November), but it ends by about 10 November and gives no cold here. ECMWF has a Greenland high on 30 November to 7 December and 14-21 December, in the extended range only.

🟡 Cold air in place upwind: Moscow and Kyiv have 100% of members at -8 °C at 850 hPa on 7 November, but both sit south-east of our track. Oslo reaches only 10% and Stockholm 12% by 19-21 November, with snow cover in at most 8% of members. The Eurasian snow extent is 14.55 against 16.06 million km² (rank 41 of 61).

⬜ Cold enough aloft (850 hPa about -8 °C): Copenhagen has at most 2% of members at -8 °C up to 21 November, and Oslo at most 10%. With the North Sea at +0.99 °C (57% of cells more than 1 °C above normal), the coast needs -8 °C or colder for snow rather than sleet.

⬜ It happens more than once, or lasts: no qualifying spell yet (data to 1 November). The ECMWF regimes go from block to Atlantic Ridge to NAO+ (41-49% on 15-24 November). A second block appears only in the extended range, at 45-51% for Blocking plus NAO- on 27 November to 10 December.

🟡 El Niño's grip loosens: the ocean does not. Niño 3.4 is +3.4 °C, the ONI is +2.46, and SEAS5 peaks near +4.0 °C in December and January. But AAM fell from +3.55 sd on 20 September to +0.52 sd on 6 November, and the GWO is weak in phase 7 (amplitude 0.77). For now, the atmosphere is less in the El Niño state.

months.notes: A cold first half and a mild, stormy second half. High pressure and a northerly component give frost and fog on 10-16 November, with the ECMWF week to 16 November about 2 °C below normal. From about 14-15 November, Atlantic fronts bring rain and strong winds, with a deep low over Scotland in the week to 23 November. Late November stays unsettled. SEAS5 point data: 37% of members milder. Normal is 1.1 snow days, mostly on the hills.

The upper vortex is stronger than normal (about 37-43 m/s against a model climate of 33-35 m/s), and the QBO is westerly. The ECMWF weeklies keep England 0 to +1 °C and Scotland near normal. The risk to the call: Blocking plus NAO- at 45-51% to 10 December and a Greenland high on the weekly maps, which can bring a northerly and hill snow. SEAS5 point data: 45% of members milder, 88 mm against 77 mm. Normal is 3.4 snow days.

A transition month. The strong vortex and the westerly QBO favour westerlies, but SEAS5 November has an NAO median of -1.9. SEAS5 point data: 55% of members milder, 9 frost days against 8.2. SSW chance 15%. Normal is 4.7 snow days.

My best cold month of the core winter. SEAS5 November has an NAO median of -3.0, with high pressure over Greenland and low pressure over the UK in DJF. SEAS5 point data: 49% of members milder, 10 frost days against 8.3 and 69 mm against 62 mm. I keep it at near normal, because the SEAS5 terciles are warm and the continent upwind is mild. SSW chance 22%. Normal is 3.8 snow days.

SEAS5 November has an NAO median of -2.4. Its point data has 37% of members milder and 8 frost days against 5.7. A late cold spell is possible if a February block stays. The SEAS5 JFM tercile map stays warm. Normal is 3.2 snow days.

drivers: Polar vortex: 2.5 m/s at 60°N, 10 hPa in the analysis on 7 November, 23.3 m/s below the mean for the date. NASA had 1.3 m/s on 4 November, a record low. The wind turns easterly in 100% of ECMWF ENS, AIFS ENS (machine learning), GEFS and GEPS members on about 10-12 November. All deterministic models agree. It rebuilds to 14-27 m/s by 21-23 November and to about 37-43 m/s by 4-21 December.

Depth: deep on the polar cap (10 hPa +4.25 sd, 100 hPa +1.83 sd, 100% of members above +1 sd today) but shallow on the 50 hPa wind (6.6 m/s ensemble mean, 0% of members easterly). After 15 November the share of members above +1 sd at 100 hPa is 25-39% in ECMWF ENS, up to 41% in AIFS ENS and GEPS and 0-3% in GEFS. The GFS troposphere cap turns negative by 22 November, so the surface link is short.

Shape: split-type wave 2 first (585-596 m on 2 November, tilted 33-35° west with height), then a displacement (wave 1 at 769-839 m on 13-19 November). The ECMWF ENS-mean vortex sits off the pole towards northern Europe on 12 November and back near the pole on 22 November. A weak split-type structure (85-190 m) returns in HRES and AIFS on 18-21 November.

Heat flux at 100 hPa: 32-40 K m/s on 2-4 November, 13.3 K m/s today and near normal. ECMWF HRES has a new pulse of 26.5 K m/s on 21 November, but GFS and AIFS stay below 19 K m/s. One run only, so it is an early signal.

AO/NAO: observed AO -0.66 and NAO -0.05 on 6 November. GEFS means reach -1.74 (AO) on 12 November and -1.14 (NAO) on 13 November, with 97-100% of members negative, then return near 0 by 17-18 November.

Weather regimes: ECMWF has Blocking to 9 November, Atlantic Ridge on 10-14 November, NAO+ at 41-49% on 15-24 November, and Blocking plus NAO- at 45-51% on 27 November to 10 December. Simon Lee's index agrees on the end of the block about 10-12 November and leans NAO- (about +0.6 sd) in December.
Super El Niño: Niño 3.4 +3.4 °C, ONI +2.46, SEAS5 peak near +4.0 °C in December and January. It favours a mild, stormy early winter and a negative-NAO tilt late in the winter.
QBO westerly at both levels (+15.91 m/s at 30 hPa, +13.45 m/s at 50 hPa in October): it favours a fast vortex rebuild and fewer mid-winter SSWs.
MJO: phase 4, amplitude down to 0.57 on 2 November. Weak, so no weight.

AAM: +0.52 sd on 6 November, down 0.92 in a week and the lowest in 90 days. The GWO is in phase 7 with amplitude 0.77, so it is weak. The fall supports ridges and blocks about 13-20 November. Background only.

North Atlantic SST (OISST, against 1991-2020): tripole -1.35, the positive-NAO pattern. North Sea +0.99 °C: heavier showers in an easterly but marginal snow at the coast. Barents-Kara +1.96 °C: linked to a weak vortex. GOES boxes (against 2003 on): Gulf Stream +0.41 °C, Sargasso +0.98 °C.

Snow cover and the cold pool: Eurasian extent 14.55 against 16.06 million km² (rank 41 of 61). The cold reaches Moscow and Kyiv (100% at -8 °C at 850 hPa on 7 November) but only 10-12% of members over Oslo and Stockholm by 19-21 November, with little snow cover.

Seasonal models: the October maps (C3S, SEAS5, GloSea) were run before the event and show the UK +0.5 to +1 °C. The SEAS5 November issue has warm terciles for Scotland but a strongly negative NAO (medians -1.6 to -3.0 from November to February) and a Greenland high in DJF MSLP. I weight the NAO signal up. Its raw point data has about half of the DJF members colder than normal.

Analogs: the autumn-matched five (mean DJF +0.3 °C) and the four early-SSW winters (mean -0.3 °C) are both within chance, so they do not move the odds. None had a November reversal. CET: a cold November is followed by a cold DJF 38% of the time against 33%.

Met Office (11 November to 5 December): a cold, dry start, then Atlantic fronts from the weekend of 14-15 November, and above normal after. I agree on the timing, but I expect near normal in Scotland in early December. AER (2 November): a record early SSW and a long disruption. I agree on the SSW, but both the 10 hPa and the 100 hPa signals fade by late November.

Polar vortex strength: zonal-mean zonal wind at 60°N (m/s, daily UTC mean, positive = westerly) at 10 hPa (the standard SSW level: a reversal to easterly is a major sudden stratospheric warming) and 50 hPa (lower stratosphere), per model; ensembles give mean/p10/p90/min across members and the % of members easterly. Early-warning signs from the single runs: polar_cap_t10 = area-mean temperature over 60-90°N at 10 hPa (°C; a jump of 20 °C or more in a few days is a sudden warming under way), heat_flux_100 = eddy heat flux v'T' around 60°N at 100 hPa (K m/s; sustained high values push wave energy up and tend to weaken the vortex 1-2 weeks later), waves_10hPa = amplitude in metres of zonal wavenumber 1 and 2 in the 10 hPa geopotential height around 60°N (wave 1 growing to well over 1000 m means the vortex is being displaced off the pole; wave 2 growing to several hundred metres means it is being stretched towards a split; in winter a few hundred metres each is ordinary; waves_vs_season places today against this season's analysed days). wave2_by_level gives, per single run and day, the longitude (°E, 0-180; the second ridge is 180° further east) of the wave-2 ridges in the 60°N height at 500, 100 and 10 hPa, their amplitudes, and the tilt (10 hPa ridge minus 500 hPa ridge): a ridge that shifts west with height (negative tilt, e.g. 45°E at 500, 29°E at 100, 6°E at 10 hPa) with ridges near the Urals and Alaska is the structure of a split. For ensembles, pct_members_ever_easterly is the share of members that reverse on any day of the run (the SSW probability for that window; the per-day share understates it) and reversal_median_date the typical timing. Days before 2026-11-07 are analysis.

periods.text: At the start of this period, outbreaks of rain across the south of the UK will clear away as clearer conditions spread from the north. A few wintry showers are likely in the far north, but otherwise this will mean a spell of fine and dry weather developing for most areas at the end of next week and the weekend. Over the following week, a change to more changeable weather is likely, with Atlantic frontal systems bringing rain and some strong winds. After a cold start, temperatures will probably be above average overall.

Changeable or unsettled conditions are expected through the last part of November. Atlantic frontal system are likely to spread across the UK, bringing some heavy rain at times and a chance of strong winds. Drier, brighter interludes are likely between systems, and it is possible conditions could become drier overall into early December. Temperatures are likely to be above normal overall.
